title: Escaping the Diversity Trap in Robotic Manipulation via Anchor-Centric Adaptation
claim: Spreading a fixed budget over many unique conditions backfires; concentrating repeated samples on a few anchors gives an optimal interior trade-off.
layout: 3 stacked rows: top side-by-side photos, middle curve, bottom three 3D surfaces
description: The top row has two side-by-side real-robot photos of a white arm over a tabletop. Left, titled "Small Budget, Max Coverage", has scattered orange cubes with red dashed one-shot trajectories, a confused thought bubble with a question mark, and the label "One Demo Each". Right, titled "Anchor Repetition & Expansion", has blue glowing rings at a few anchor cubes with dense blue repeated trajectories, a green check bubble, and the label "Repeated Anchors". Below is a green inverted-U curve of success rate against number of anchors, with circle markers. Dashed pink and blue arrows link points on the curve to the photos above and to three 3D density surfaces below. The surfaces are labeled no anchors, 4 anchors and 9 anchors. They show a noisy flat landscape, a few tall peaks, and many peaks. Warm red and cool blue contrast the two strategies.
caption: Illustration of Motivation. Top: Contrasting the "diversity trap" of sparse, single-shot sampling against stable anchor-centric repetition. Middle & Bottom: Inverted-U trend of success versus number of anchors, with 3D visualizations of sample distributions and densities at representative points.
abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer broad general capabilities, deploying them on specific hardware requires real-world adaptation to bridge the embodiment gap. Since robot demonstrations are costly, this adaptation must often occur under a strict data budget. In this work, we identify a critical diversity trap: the standard heuristic of "maximizing coverage" by collecting diverse, single-shot demonstrations can be self-defeating due to non-vanishing estimation noise. We formalize this phenomenon as a Coverage--Density Trade-off. By decomposing the policy error into estimation (density) and extrapolation (coverage) terms, we characterize an interior optimal allocation of unique conditions for a fixed budget. Guided by this analysis, we propose Anchor-Centric Adaptation (ACA), a two-stage framework that first stabilizes a policy skeleton through repeated demonstrations at core anchors, then selectively expands coverage to high-risk boundaries via teacher-forced error mining and constrained residual updates. Real-robot experiments validate our trade-off framework and demonstrate that ACA significantly improves task reliability and success rates over standard diverse sampling strategies under the same budget.
